title: Ancestors and Teachers Part 2
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk highlights the importance of integrating practice and realization in Buddhist teachings, a direction emphasized by H.O., the second abbot of Eiji and a key figure in preserving Dogen's teachings. This approach, which emphasizes the dynamic and living nature of the Dharma, is reflected in Dogen's writings, such as the Sui Monki, which offer a more direct and accessible path to understanding his teachings. By studying and engaging with these writings, practitioners can deepen their understanding of the Buddha's teachings and carry forward the tradition in a way that is both authentic and responsible.

sentences.text: Good evening.
I had lots of great ideas on what to do with this dharma talk.
Unfortunately, I tried to throw them all together into one pot, so it may not be my most coherent talk ever.
This is the second talk about teachers and ancestors, and I have to make a confession.
Whenever I consider buying a book, I read the first few pages, and then I read the last few pages.
I know for some people this is practically a criminal offense.
They would never dream of finding out how the book ends before reading the beginning.
But I want to know where the writer is taking me.
And if I don't like the ending, I may decide that the journey isn't worth the trouble.
Of course, I'm probably wrong a lot, too.
So when I was thinking about whom to introduce as our first individual ancestor in this series, I went to the end of the book.
Koan H.O. was the final named master in Kaisan's Denko Roku, the record of the transmission of the light.
He was the final one in the list, and he was Dogen's successor.
He was the second abbot at Eiji, and a man who did an enormous amount of work to preserve Dogen's teachings for future generations.
Without H.O., we might know way less about Dogen than we do today.
We might not really know much about Dogen at all, because it's not only the founder of the tradition who determines the final outcome of it, but the people carrying it forward.
It's like Christianity becoming popular under Paul, who never even saw Jesus.
But he was the one who turned it into a tradition that was acceptable to many.
So, you might wonder why I begin the series about the ancestors at the end of the book, Transmission of Illumination, or Transmission of Light.
Transmission of Light was translated by Thomas Cleary, and this one here is, I believe, the official Soto Zen record of Transmission of Illumination.
So I think it's appropriate to start with H.O.
He wasn't the founder of a new school.
He did not become famous for any [unclear: "traumatic"] encounters with students or for the kind of outrageous behavior that makes some of the old Zen stories so much fun.
His contribution was quiet, but no less important.
He received the teaching.
He made it his own and helped carry it into the future.
There's something else I find very interesting about H.O.
Before he met Dogen, he was already a serious and accomplished Buddhist practitioner.
He had studied in several traditions and spent years exploring the Dharma.
He was not waiting around for a great teacher to tell him what to do.
He was already on his own journey.
I like to think of H.O. as an explorer who had traveled through different landscapes, studied different maps, and learned a great deal along the way.
But then he encountered Dogen, and something in Dogen's teaching gave him a new orientation.
Dogen became his North Star, not someone who dictated every step, but someone whose understanding helped H.O. recognize the direction in which he wanted to travel.
Tonight, together with you, I would like to explore what happened when that North Star was there, and then when it was no longer there.
And H.O. did carry on.
Okay, is this better?
H.O. was born in Kyoto in 1198, so he was a couple of years older than Dogen.
He was part of an aristocratic family, the Fuchibaras.
He lived during a period of enormous political and religious change in Japan.
The old aristocratic order was losing power to the emerging warrior government, and new forms of Buddhism were challenging the authority of established religious institutions.
At 18, H.O. entered the Great Tendai Buddhist Establishment on Mount Hiei.
He studied Buddhist philosophy and doctrine, and apparently showed considerable promise as a scholar.
But then his mother visited him and asked him to promise not to return to Hiei.
So H.O. established himself as an elite disciple in Kakuon's Daruma school.
Daruma means Bodhidharma.
However, his path took an abrupt turn in 1228.
Monks from Konfuku-ji, the powerful Tendai center in Nara, set fire to the Daruma school complex.
It was apparently an argument over its emerging prominence.
The monastery was destroyed, forcing the community of practitioners to scatter.
Dogen and H.O. probably met first somewhere around 1227, and H.O. had studied different approaches to liberation and worked with different teachers.
Again, I would like to emphasize that he was not necessarily waiting for someone new to teach him.
I want to emphasize this because our transmission stories, also the stories of the Denko Voku, sometimes give the impression that a student knows nothing until a teacher appears.
We all bring our whole self and all of our experiences and lived history to our practice, and that was also true of H.O.
However, H.O. recognized something in Dogen's teaching due to the journey he had already undertaken.
Like us, he did not arrive as a blank slate.
We bring our histories, our relationships, our accomplishments and failures, our confusion to practice.
And sometimes we encounter a teaching or a teacher, a phrase or a sentence that can change the direction of our life.
But that teaching does not erase all that came before.
However, it may allow us to see it in a different light.
To bring you back to Buddhist history in Japan, Dogen returned from China in 1227, bringing with him a particular understanding of Zen practice shaped by his training with the Chinese master Rujing.
Dogen taught that practice and realization were not two separate things.
We do not practice in order to acquire enlightenment at some future time; just this, right now.
Practice itself is the expression of awakening, and this was not merely a philosophical position.
Dogen insisted that the Buddha way was expressed through the whole of our lives, through zazen, eating, working, washing, and our relationships with one another.
For someone like H.O., who had spent years exploring different approaches, this understanding must have been compelling.
Perhaps it brought together things he had been struggling to reconcile.
Perhaps it challenged assumptions he had carried.
We don't know, and we don't need to know.
H.O. did not immediately become Dogen's disciple.
Several years passed before he joined Dogen's community in Kojō-ji in 1234.
In 1235, he formally received the Bodhisattva precepts from Dogen.
In 1236, he received Dharma transmission and served as the community's first shusō.
Think about that.
Here was a man who had already spent nearly 20 years studying and practicing Buddhism.
He had been a respected practitioner in other communities, yet he was absolutely willing to begin again, to enter a new community and take up its forms.
I find that deeply moving.
There is a kind of maturity that allows us to recognize when something is worth changing our lives for, to begin anew, to start at the bottom.
And there is another kind of maturity that allows us to do so without needing to reject everything that came before.
I think this is something we can also recognize in our own lives.

We may have spent years approaching something in a particular way, perhaps believing that we understood what mattered, and then we encounter a person, a teaching, or an experience that fundamentally changes our orientation.
The old map is no longer sufficient.
That does not mean that the journey up to that point is wasted.
It just means the journey continues in a different direction.
H.O. served Dogen as an attendant, but we should not imagine him simply following Dogen around, carrying his belongings and waiting for instructions.
H.O. was a senior practitioner and teacher in his own right, and yet it is said in the Transmission of Light that he stuck to Dogen like a shadow.
Wherever he went, H.O. went with him.
That was no small undertaking.
They were establishing a monastery in a remote region.
Buildings had to be constructed, food and supplies obtained, schedules organized, and relationships maintained.
And someone, or many someones, had to make all of that work.
I think sometimes we have a rather romantic picture of the old Zen masters and what it was like.
Just remember that they tried to frame the Buddha for murder, and that H.O. lost the monastery because another monastery burned it down because it was competition.
So let's take off our rose-colored glasses and appreciate how civilized we are most of the time.
So part of H.O.'s great contribution is his work preserving Dogen's teaching.
H.O. recorded many of Dogen's informal talks.
He eventually became the Shogun Sui Monki, often translated as the record of things heard from the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
And if you have ever struggled through some of Dogen's more difficult writings, I recommend the Sui Monki.
Here we encounter a somewhat different Dogen.
He speaks directly to his students about their lives, their ambitions, their difficulties.
He talks about fame and gain, about letting go of self-centered concerns, and about the very ordinary way we get caught in our preferences.
There is a directness in those talks.
It makes them particularly accessible, so you might enjoy them.
I know that Scott is a big fan.
And we have all these talks because H.O. listened.
H.O. also helped copy, organize, and preserve Dogen's lecture writings, including the Shobogenzo.
But H.O. wasn't simply preserving Dogen's words.
He was helping create a place where those words could be lived and where they could continue to live on.
And perhaps that is an interesting picture of lineage.
Then a series of masters handing enlightenment down through the centuries.
It's a picture of people practicing together, each contributing something that the others could not do alone.
In the early 1250s, Dogen became very ill.
By the summer of 1253, it was clear that his health was failing.
He entrusted the leadership of Ehechi to H.O. and traveled to Kyoto in hopes of receiving medical treatment.
Dogen died in Kyoto in 1253, at the age of 53.
And H.O. brought his teacher's remains back to Ehechi.
For nearly 20 years, H.O. had been Dogen's shadow.
He had helped establish the community, recorded his teachings, assisted him in ceremonies, and shared the daily life.
Dogen had become a central orientation of his religious life.
And now Dogen was dead.
We don't know much about H.O.'s private grief.
The traditional accounts emphasize his devotion and succession to the [unclear: "apathy"].
But they don't give us much access to his experience.
But I think we can recognize the situation.
Someone who has profoundly influenced our life is no longer there.
Someone whose presence helped orient us, whose understanding we trusted.
Now he was gone.
I don't think H.O. needed Dogen to tell him what to do.
But there's a difference between being capable of making our own decisions and having someone whose presence helps us see more clearly.
The North Star helps us find our direction.
But if we spend all our time staring at that star, we will never actually travel anywhere.
Eventually we have to walk.
I wonder if this was, in a sense, the task that faced H.O.: not to become another Dogen, not to imitate his teacher's personality, but to continue walking in his chosen direction.
Like I said, after Dogen's death, H.O. became the second abbot of Ehechi.
He was responsible for what he had helped to build that was still young, a community that had lost its founding teacher.
So there was something [unclear: "fighting.
Different that H.O. was more their compatriot than their abbot"].
And there's about 14 years that he held on to the abbessy.
And then due to his declining health, he left.
And surprise, surprise, he got a lot better once he had all that stress off his plate.
I loved the relationship that H.O. had with Dogen.
So that was one thing I was trying to do tonight.
The other is to make you familiar with a couple of the books that are usually used to study the old teachers.
This is a translation of the Denko Roku, Transmission of Light, a record of transmission of illumination.
This one is by Thomas Cleary.
It's very accessible.
This is the same, but the font is way, way, way, way smaller.
The pages are a lot smaller, and the pages are a lot thinner.
I want to give you a taste of the difference in how Griffith Folk, who was the editor-in-chief for this, and Cleary tackled the material.
So I'll just read a little section out of each one so you get a sense of what it's like.
*H.O. studied with Zen Master Dogen.
One day in the course of inquiries he heard the saying, "One hair goes through myriad holes."
And all of a sudden realized enlightenment.
That evening he went to Dogen and said, "I do not ask about one hair.
What about the myriad holes?"
Dogen smiled and said, "Gone through.
What about?"*
And then it tells you a little bit about him growing up.
So no footnotes, very straightforward, lovely.
And now chapter 52.
I have the right one.
*The 52nd ancestor, Reverend A.H.O., sought instruction from Reverend Dogen.
One day during the rite of requesting edification, A.H.O. heard the episode of a single hair [unclear: "pieces"] multiple holes and thereby had an introspective awakening.
In the evening he made [unclear: "frustrations"] to Dogen and said, "I do not ask about a single hair, but what are the multiple holes?"
Dogen smiled slightly and said, "Pierced."
Master A.H.O. made [unclear: "frustrations"].*
And then it gives you the same in Japanese.
And then footnotes.
I want to read just one footnote here.
The footnote is about the episode of a single hair piercing multiple holes.
*This is a famous koan found in many Chan Zen texts, including the Record of the Transmission of the Flame and Dogen's Treasury of the True Dharma Eye in Chinese characters.
The koan involves Shishuan Kunzhu, who was asked, "What about when a single hair pierces multiple holes?"
His reply and that of many other Chan Zen masters, who subsequently commented on the case, amount to an interpretation of the meaning of the question itself, which is far from clear.
The expression "single hair," also translated here in as "an iota," represents the smallest conceivable thing in the universe.
To believe that any such thing exists is a fundamental conclusion that Chan Zen masters strive to disabuse their students of.
As Kaisan says in Chapter 42 of the Dengaroku, "In awakening, there will be not an iota of anything to attain," which equals a single hair piercing multiple holes.*

So that's just one footnote out of this version, which makes it to me way more entertaining and interesting, because I don't want to reinvent the wheel, especially if I don't know anything about the wheel.
It's from a foreign culture and I just end up stumped, so I really do enjoy this book very much.
And there's also a book of the same size, which is just footnotes, so welcome to Geekdom.
I really wanted to show you the difference between the two works, and Thomas Clear is a wonderful entry.
There's one last thing I would like to say, which is that the Dharma is not a museum.
It's not that we're trying to maintain something in a fixed form, that we hold onto it tightly, just carrying on without it having sense and meaning in our lives, not letting anyone touch it.

It's carrying it forward carefully, mindfully, attentively, with an understanding that it is meant to be used. [unclear: "Age of Preserve tokens writings"], but he also helped create the conditions in which those teachings could continue to be practiced.
And this very much reminds me of Shunryu Suzuki Roshi, who came from Japan with his version of Zen, which has very little to do with what is practiced in Japan on a daily basis.
He brought us a new shape.
He didn't want us to cling to all the Japanese traditions.
And this brings me back to the question which we began with in our first talk.
Why do we remember these people?
Not because they were perfect, not because they were free from confusion, conflict, or disappointment, but definitely not that we want to become like them.
We don't want to become like them.
We want to become ourselves.
H.O. shows us that receiving the Dharma is an active undertaking.
It is not simply agreeing with a teaching or admiring a teacher.

It is allowing what we have understood to change the direction of our lives and then doing the work, and then supporting others in their practice, listening carefully, showing up, and taking responsibility.
You may think you are just sitting here, but you are the ancestors that people will look to in the future.
So let's see if we have time to do some triads.
I pose a question that you can pick up or not.
If it doesn't interest you, pick something else.
Has it happened to you that you have reoriented your life through an encounter?
Or another question might be, how do you respond when you lose your good teacher or someone who really influenced your life?
Or maybe, what does it mean to carry forward a teaching?
So if you could find groups of three.
